questions.stem:
Statements: All dogs are animals. All animals are living beings.
Conclusions: I. All dogs are living beings. II. All living beings are dogs.
questions.explanation: All dogs → animals → living beings. So All dogs are living beings (I: valid). The reverse 'All living beings are dogs' cannot be concluded (II: invalid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some cats are dogs. All dogs are birds.
Conclusions: I. Some cats are birds. II. All birds are cats.
questions.explanation: Some cats are dogs + All dogs are birds → Some cats are birds (I: valid by combining particular affirmative with universal affirmative). 'All birds are cats' reverses the relationship wrongly (II: invalid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: No pen is a pencil. All pencils are erasers.
Conclusions: I. No pen is an eraser. II. Some erasers are not pens.
questions.explanation: No pen is pencil + All pencils are erasers → Some erasers are not pens (since all pencils = erasers, and no pen is pencil, so those erasers that came from pencils are not pens). Conclusion I 'No pen is an eraser' cannot be concluded since pens may still be erasers from another route.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All chairs are tables. Some tables are desks.
Conclusions: I. Some chairs are desks. II. Some desks are tables.
questions.explanation: All chairs are tables + Some tables are desks: the 'some tables' that are desks may or may not be those that are chairs — so I does not necessarily follow. 'Some desks are tables' is the converse of 'Some tables are desks' — valid (II follows).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All flowers are plants. No plant is a tree.
Conclusions: I. No flower is a tree. II. Some trees are flowers.
questions.explanation: All flowers are plants + No plant is tree → No flower is a tree (valid: A+E → E). Conclusion II 'Some trees are flowers' contradicts I and cannot follow.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some books are pens. Some pens are rulers.
Conclusions: I. Some books are rulers. II. Some rulers are books.
questions.explanation: Some + Some gives no definite conclusion. The 'some books that are pens' may or may not overlap with 'some pens that are rulers'. Neither I nor II necessarily follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All mangoes are fruits. All fruits are delicious.
Conclusions: I. All mangoes are delicious. II. All delicious things are mangoes.
questions.explanation: All mangoes → fruits → delicious. So All mangoes are delicious (I: valid). The converse 'All delicious things are mangoes' (II) cannot be derived.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some cars are buses. All buses are vehicles.
Conclusions: I. Some cars are vehicles. II. Some vehicles are cars.
questions.explanation: Some cars are buses + All buses are vehicles → Some cars are vehicles (I: valid). The converse of a particular affirmative is valid: 'Some vehicles are cars' (II: also valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: No man is a woman. All women are humans.
Conclusions: I. No man is human. II. Some humans are not men.
questions.explanation: No man is woman + All women are humans: all women are humans but men may or may not be human (I: cannot conclude 'No man is human'). Since all women are humans and no man is a woman, those women who are humans are not men — so Some humans are not men (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All A are B. No B is C. Some C are D.
Conclusions: I. No A is C. II. Some D are not B.
questions.explanation: All A→B, No B→C: so No A is C (I: valid, A+E→E). For II: Some C are D; No B is C → those Ds that come from C cannot be B → Some D are not B (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All lions are tigers. Some tigers are bears.
Conclusions: I. Some lions are bears. II. Some bears are tigers.
questions.explanation: All lions → tigers. Some tigers are bears — these 'some tigers' may or may not include those that are lions. So I (Some lions are bears) does NOT necessarily follow. Converse of 'Some tigers are bears' is 'Some bears are tigers' (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: No A is B. Some B are C.
Conclusions: I. Some C are not A. II. No C is A.
questions.explanation: No A is B → No B is A. Some B are C → those 'some B' that are C are not A → Some C are not A (I: valid). 'No C is A' is too strong — some C may be A from a different set (II: invalid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All P are Q. All Q are R. No R is S.
Conclusions: I. No P is S. II. No Q is S.
questions.explanation: All P→Q→R, No R→S: so No P is S (I: valid) and No Q is S since all Q are R and No R is S (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some students are clever. All clever people are hardworking.
Conclusion: Some students are hardworking.
questions.explanation: Some students are clever + All clever are hardworking → Some students are hardworking (I+A → I type: valid conclusion).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All X are Y. Some Y are Z. No Z is W.
Conclusions: I. Some X are Z. II. No Y is W.
questions.explanation: All X→Y; Some Y→Z: the 'some Y that are Z' may or may not include those Y that come from X → I doesn't follow. 'No Y is W': No Z is W, but Y includes elements that are NOT Z, and those non-Z Ys could be W → II doesn't follow.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All pens are books. All books are shelves.
Conclusions: I. All pens are shelves. II. All shelves are pens.
questions.explanation: All pens→books→shelves: All pens are shelves (I: valid). 'All shelves are pens' reverses a universal affirmative, which is not valid (II: invalid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some roses are red. Some red things are beautiful.
Conclusions: I. Some roses are beautiful. II. All beautiful things are red.
questions.explanation: Some+Some gives no definite conclusion. I doesn't follow (the roses that are red may not be among the red things that are beautiful). II is a universal affirmative that cannot be derived from particular premises.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All doctors are rich. No rich person is poor.
Conclusions: I. No doctor is poor. II. Some poor people are not doctors.
questions.explanation: All doctors→rich; No rich→poor: so No doctor is poor (I: valid). Since no doctor is poor, any poor person is not a doctor → Some (in fact, all) poor people are not doctors (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some teachers are singers. All singers are dancers.
Conclusions: I. Some teachers are dancers. II. Some dancers are teachers.
questions.explanation: Some teachers→singers; All singers→dancers: Some teachers are dancers (I: valid). Converse of particular affirmative: Some dancers are teachers (II: valid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All birds can fly. Penguins are birds.
Conclusions: I. Penguins can fly. II. Some birds are penguins.
questions.explanation: This is a purely logical question — assuming the statements are true (even if contrary to real life): All birds can fly + Penguins are birds → Penguins can fly (I: logically valid). 'Penguins are birds' → Some birds are penguins (II: valid conversion).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All tables are wood. Some wood is hard. No hard thing is cheap.
Conclusions: I. Some tables may be cheap. II. Some wood is not cheap.
questions.explanation: Some wood is hard + No hard is cheap → Some wood is not cheap (II: valid — the wood that is hard cannot be cheap). I says 'may be cheap' which is a possibility but given no hard thing is cheap and tables are wood, whether tables are cheap depends on whether they are the hard wood subset — the conclusion I is uncertain, not definite.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All A are B. All C are B.
Conclusions: I. All A are C. II. Some B are A.
questions.explanation: All A are B → Some B are A (valid conversion of universal affirmative to particular — II follows). All A are B and All C are B does not mean All A are C; A and C share B as a common set but may be completely different subsets of B (I: invalid).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some engineers are managers. No manager is a clerk.
Conclusions: I. Some engineers are not clerks. II. Some clerks are not engineers.
questions.explanation: Some engineers→managers; No manager→clerk: those engineers who are managers are not clerks → Some engineers are not clerks (I: valid). 'Some clerks are not engineers' — clerks may or may not include engineers from a different angle; cannot be determined from these statements alone (II: doesn't necessarily follow).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: All stars are planets. No planet is a moon.
Conclusions: I. No star is a moon. II. All planets are stars.
questions.explanation: All stars→planets; No planet→moon: No star is moon (I: valid, A+E→E). 'All planets are stars' reverses the universal affirmative, which is invalid (II: doesn't follow).
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem:
Statements: Some actors are directors. All directors are producers. Some producers are writers.
Conclusions: I. Some actors are producers. II. Some writers are directors.
questions.explanation: Some actors→directors; All directors→producers: Some actors are producers (I: valid). For II: All directors→producers and Some producers are writers — but the 'some producers' that are writers may not be those that came from directors (II: doesn't necessarily follow).
questions.subject: Reasoning
